analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Medicaid work rules, eligibility limits, and financing changes in the 2025 tax-and-spending law.
analysis.headline: A single House member introduced the bill on July 9, 2026, with no cosponsors; it was referred to two committees and has seen no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would erase the Medicaid changes enacted in the 2025 reconciliation law (Public Law 119-21). Those changes require many Medicaid enrollees to work or do community service to keep coverage, restrict Medicaid and CHIP to citizens and certain lawfully present residents, and limit the provider taxes states use to help finance Medicaid. The bill would put the old rules back in place as if the 2025 changes had never happened.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income Medicaid enrollees, including adults in the expansion population who would no longer face work or community-engagement requirements, and lawfully present immigrants who would regain or keep eligibility. Hospitals, especially safety-net hospitals, would benefit from fewer uninsured patients and less unpaid care, and state budgets would face less cost pressure.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-income Medicaid enrollees and safety-net hospitals

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the Medicaid provisions of the 2025 reconciliation law, including the requirement that people in the Medicaid expansion population perform work, community service, or similar activities to qualify for coverage.

It would restore Medicaid and CHIP eligibility to include lawfully present groups such as lawful permanent residents, Cuban-Haitian entrants, and Compact of Free Association migrants, whom the 2025 law generally excluded beginning in fiscal 2027.
It would undo the limits the 2025 law placed on the provider taxes states use to help fund their Medicaid programs.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers would bear the cost: repealing the 2025 law's Medicaid provisions restores federal spending on the program, which was a major source of the savings in that law. States that had already begun implementing the new eligibility and financing rules would also unwind those changes.

drawbacks.text: Full repeal restores Medicaid spending the 2025 law had cut, adding to federal deficits, since the Medicaid savings helped pay for that law's tax provisions.

Repealing the provider-tax limits also restores a state financing practice that critics have long described as shifting costs to federal taxpayers, so some of the restored spending does not buy new care.

Supporters of the 2025 law argued the work and eligibility rules encourage self-sufficiency and limit coverage for people present without authorization; this bill would reverse all of that wholesale rather than keeping any of it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to low-income enrollees is direct and large: work requirements and eligibility restrictions reliably cause people to lose coverage, and hospitals and states absorb the spillover. The cost is real but diffuse — higher federal deficits — and the bill's wholesale repeal means it also revives the provider-tax financing games that even some Medicaid supporters have criticized. The bill was never designed to move; it is a single-sponsor statement with no cosponsors and no committee action.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to two House committees in July 2026, and neither committee has acted on it since.

narrative.text: Rep. Brendan Boyle introduced H.R. 9623 on July 9, 2026, to repeal the Medicaid-related portions of Public Law 119-21, the reconciliation act commonly called the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
The bill had zero cosponsors as of the record provided.

It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and, in addition, to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced; the action history shows no markup, hearing, or vote since.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The 2025 Medicaid changes remain in place, preserving the federal savings that helped fund that law's tax cuts. People who would have lost coverage under those changes, and the hospitals and states that would have absorbed the cost, are worse off for the bill going nowhere.

sides.party_line_note: A single House Democrat introduced the bill, drew zero cosponsors of either party, and the Republican majority that enacted the 2025 Medicaid provisions controls the committees that would have to move it.

industries.note: The 2025 law's eligibility restrictions and work requirements increase the number of uninsured patients whose care hospitals must absorb unpaid. Repealing them restores coverage and eases the financial strain that has contributed to rural hospital closures.

Repeal reverses enrollment losses the work requirements and eligibility restrictions would otherwise cause, keeping more covered lives — and premiums — in state Medicaid programs run through private insurers.
The bill would remove the provider-tax limits and eligibility rules that shift costs onto state budgets, reducing the pressure states face from the 2025 law's changes.

analysis.trajectory: With no cosponsors, no committee action, and a majority whose 2025 law the bill would partly dismantle, this bill has no realistic path to a vote; the most likely outcome is that it dies quietly at the end of this Congress.
